quick: 20 IU/kg once, with the first dose of rabies vaccine
Not contraindicated; give when indicated (rabies is fatal)
Wound, hypersensitivity reactions; ensure full vaccine series
summary: Rabies immune globulin (human), HRIG, provides immediate passive immunity for post-exposure prophylaxis of rabies in previously unvaccinated people. The single dose is 20 IU/kg, given once at the start of management together with the first dose of rabies vaccine. As much as anatomically feasible is infiltrated around and into the bite wound(s), and any remainder is given intramuscularly at a site distant from the vaccine. It bridges protection until the patient's own vaccine-induced antibodies develop and must never replace the vaccine.
indications: Post-exposure prophylaxis of rabies, together with rabies vaccine, in persons not previously immunized against rabies

dosage.d: 20 IU/kg body weight as a single dose
dosage.n: Give with the first vaccine dose; do not exceed the recommended dose (excess may suppress vaccine response)

dosage.d: Infiltrate as much of the 20 IU/kg dose as anatomically feasible around/into the wound(s)
dosage.n: Inject remainder IM at a site distant from the vaccine site

dosage.c: Persons already fully vaccinated against rabies

admin: Infiltrate as much of the calculated dose as feasible into and around the bite wound(s)
Administer any remaining volume intramuscularly, in the gluteal region or anterolateral thigh, distant from the vaccine injection site
NEVER give in the same syringe or anatomic site as the rabies vaccine, and use a separate needle/syringe
Give once, at or as soon as possible after the start of post-exposure prophylaxis; if not given with the first vaccine dose, it can be given up to day 7 of the vaccine series (not later)
moa: Rabies immune globulin contains preformed neutralizing IgG antibodies against rabies virus, derived from pooled plasma of hyperimmunized human donors. Local infiltration around the wound neutralizes virus at the site of entry before it reaches the nervous system, while circulating antibody provides immediate systemic passive protection. This covers the interval (about 7-10 days) before active vaccine-induced immunity develops; it does not stimulate the patient's own immune response.

absolute: There are essentially no contraindications when rabies exposure has occurred, because untreated rabies is almost universally fatal
relative: Prior systemic hypersensitivity to human immune globulin preparations
IgA deficiency with antibodies to IgA (risk of reaction)
Do not give to persons already completely immunized with a rabies vaccine series
monitor: Patients with bleeding disorders/thrombocytopenia (IM injection bleeding risk)
History of adverse reactions to blood products

preg: Rabies is nearly always fatal, so pregnancy is not a contraindication; rabies immune globulin (and vaccine) should be given when post-exposure prophylaxis is indicated.
lact: Breastfeeding is not a contraindication; rabies immune globulin may be given to nursing mothers when indicated.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in renal impairment.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

major: Do not exceed the 20 IU/kg dose - excess immune globulin can partially suppress the active antibody response to the rabies vaccine
moderate: Live attenuated virus vaccines (e.g. measles, mumps, rubella, varicella) - passive antibodies can blunt the response; defer such vaccines for an appropriate interval (commonly ~3-4 months)
minor: Corticosteroids/immunosuppressants - may impair the active vaccine response (give the full prophylaxis regardless)
interactions.diagnostics: Passively transferred antibodies may cause transient positive results in some serologic tests.

rare: Theoretical transmission of blood-borne infectious agents (donor plasma derived)

monitoring: Observe for immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reactions after administration
Ensure the full rabies vaccine series is completed on schedule
Adequacy and timing of post-exposure prophylaxis per public-health guidance
counsel: This injection gives immediate antibody protection while the vaccine takes effect - you still need every dose of the rabies vaccine on schedule
Most of the dose is injected around the bite wound; some soreness, swelling or mild fever is expected
Tell the clinician about any allergy to blood products or immunoglobulins, or any bleeding disorder
After receiving this, certain live vaccines (e.g. MMR, varicella) may need to be delayed - inform your doctor
pk: Bridges protection for ~7-10 days until vaccine immunity develops
pearls: Give HRIG only once and only to previously unvaccinated people - already-vaccinated patients get booster vaccine alone
Infiltrate as much as feasible around the wound to neutralize virus at the entry site; inject the rest IM far from the vaccine site, using a separate syringe
Never exceed 20 IU/kg - too much immune globulin can blunt the active vaccine response
Wound care plus prompt vaccine plus HRIG is the standard; if HRIG was missed it can still be given up to day 7 of the vaccine course
Defer live-virus vaccines (MMR, varicella) for a few months after HRIG
missed: Rabies immune globulin is ideally given on day 0 with the first vaccine dose. If it was not given then, it can still be administered through day 7 of the vaccine series; it is NOT given after day 7 (the patient's own antibody response is presumed to have begun). Do not delay seeking prophylaxis after any potential rabies exposure.
overdose: Doses above the recommended 20 IU/kg offer no extra benefit and may suppress the vaccine-induced antibody response. There is no specific antidote; manage any reactions supportively.
